lines: Brand-new parts cost a fortune around here. Before you pay that, check the bays one more time, there's usually a better road.
Shop price on that one, and it hurts. I only sell new when the scrap pile has nothing left to give.
A fresh part at full condition, priced like a luxury. Fine if you're desperate, but I'd rather see you squeeze the old ones first.

report.reason: Lines 1 and 2 carry a dry, cheeky grin and are not mean. Line 3 is more flat and slightly scolding ('I'd rather see you squeeze the old ones first'), but it still shows pride in squeezing parts and is not mean.

Line 3 says 'priced like a luxury' and 'full condition', which brings in a rich, premium feel. It is used as a complaint about the price, but it still leans toward wealth. Lines 1 and 2 keep the underpaid, scrappy tone.
Only the player/mechanic is present. No other mechanics, crew, boss or successor.

All three treat buying new as expensive and a last resort. Line 2 says new only when the scrap pile has nothing left. Line 1 says check the bays again. Line 3 says fine if desperate. None spells out the swap trick.

Line 1's 'check the bays one more time, there's usually a better road' and line 3's 'squeeze the old ones first' are nudges, not explanations. Line 1 comes closest, since 'check the bays' hints at looking at the ships, but it does not tell the player to move parts or name any levels.
report.evidence: check the bays one more time, there's usually a better road

report.reason: The lines use only the game's world: new parts, bays, scrap pile, shop. No invented places, factions or tech.
